cdg.title: What is CDG?
cdg.text: Congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG) are a large group of rare genetic conditions. They affect how the body attaches sugar chains (glycans) to proteins and fats — a process almost every cell depends on. Because of this, CDG can affect many organs at once: the brain, muscles, liver, eyes and heart.

autism.eyebrow: A different way of experiencing the world
autism.title: What is autism?
autism.text: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition that shapes how a person communicates, interacts with others and experiences the world. It is a spectrum: every autistic person has their own strengths and needs, and early, individual support makes a real difference.

cdg.title: Congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG)
cdg.lead: CDG is a family of more than 130 rare, inherited metabolic conditions. Most children are diagnosed in infancy, and symptoms can range from mild to severe.

sections.title: What is CDG?
paragraphs: Congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG) are a large group of rare genetic disorders that affect glycosylation — the process of adding sugar building blocks, called glycans, to proteins and fats in cells throughout the body.

Glycans help proteins fold correctly, travel to the right place and do their job. When glycosylation does not work properly, many body systems can be affected at the same time. CDG is not related to diabetes, even though it involves sugars.
The most common type is PMM2-CDG (formerly called CDG-Ia). Each type is named after the gene that causes it.

sections.title: Causes
paragraphs: CDG is caused by changes (variants) in genes that control glycosylation. More than 400 genes take part in this process, and changes in over 130 of them are known to cause CDG.

Most types are inherited in an autosomal recessive way: a child is affected when they receive a non-working copy of the gene from both parents. Parents are usually healthy carriers. When both parents are carriers, each pregnancy has a 25% chance of being affected.
A few types are inherited in other ways (autosomal dominant or X-linked), and some happen because of a new (de novo) change in the child’s genes.

sections.title: Signs and symptoms
paragraphs: Symptoms vary a lot between types and even between children with the same type. They often appear in infancy and may include:
list: Low muscle tone (hypotonia) and developmental delay
Feeding difficulties and poor growth
Crossed or misaligned eyes (strabismus) and vision problems
Unusual fat distribution, inverted nipples or other physical features
Liver problems and blood clotting abnormalities
Seizures and stroke-like episodes
Balance and coordination problems (ataxia)
Heart, kidney or hormone problems
sections.after: In older children and adults, problems with balance, speech, puberty, spine curvature (scoliosis), joint stiffness and vision may become more noticeable.

sections.title: Diagnosis
paragraphs: Because CDG is rare and symptoms overlap with other conditions, diagnosis can take time. A doctor may suspect CDG when a child has problems in several body systems at once.

A blood test called transferrin glycosylation analysis (isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry) can show abnormal glycans. The exact type is then confirmed with genetic testing — a gene panel, exome or genome sequencing.
Once the family’s genetic variant is known, genetic counselling can help parents understand the chance of CDG in future pregnancies.

sections.title: Treatment and care
paragraphs: For most types of CDG there is no cure yet, so care focuses on managing symptoms and supporting development. A team of specialists usually works together:
list: Neurologist, geneticist and metabolic specialist
Nutrition support, sometimes including a feeding tube
Physical, occupational and speech therapy
Seizure medication when needed
Monitoring of the liver, blood clotting, heart and hormones
Eye care, glasses and orthopaedic support
sections.after: A few types can be treated directly: for example, MPI-CDG responds to oral mannose, and some other types may benefit from specific sugar supplements. Research into new therapies is ongoing worldwide.

sections.title: Outlook
paragraphs: The outlook depends on the type of CDG and how severe it is. Some children have mild symptoms, while others need lifelong care and regular follow-up.
With early diagnosis, coordinated medical care, therapy and a supportive community, many children with CDG make steady progress and enjoy a good quality of life.

autism.title: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)
autism.lead: Autism is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition. It is not an illness to be cured, but a different way of thinking, communicating and experiencing the world — one that deserves understanding and the right support.

sections.title: What is autism?
paragraphs: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects how a person communicates, interacts with other people, and processes information from their senses. The word “spectrum” means that autism looks different in every person — some people need a lot of daily support, while others live fully independently.
According to the World Health Organization, about 1 in 100 children worldwide is autistic. Autism is diagnosed more often in boys than in girls.

sections.title: Causes
paragraphs: There is no single cause of autism. Research shows that genetics plays the largest role, together with factors that affect early brain development before birth.
Autism is not caused by parenting, and large scientific studies have shown that vaccines do not cause autism.
Autism can occur on its own or together with other conditions, including some rare genetic disorders such as CDG, Fragile X syndrome or Phelan-McDermid syndrome.

sections.title: Early signs
paragraphs: Signs usually appear in the first two to three years of life. Parents may notice that their child:
list: Rarely makes eye contact or responds to their name
Does not point, wave or share interest with others
Has delayed speech or loses words they used before
Repeats movements, sounds or phrases
Strongly prefers routines and is upset by changes
Is very sensitive — or not sensitive — to sounds, lights, textures or pain
Has intense, focused interests
sections.after: Having one of these signs does not mean a child is autistic. If you are worried, talk to your paediatrician — early evaluation is always better than waiting.

sections.title: Diagnosis
paragraphs: There is no blood test for autism. It is diagnosed by specialists — such as a child neurologist, child psychiatrist or developmental psychologist — who observe the child’s behaviour and development and talk with the family.
Screening questionnaires such as the M-CHAT can be used at routine check-ups between 18 and 24 months. Autism can be reliably diagnosed from around the age of two.

sections.title: Support and therapy
paragraphs: Every autistic child is different, so support should be built around their individual strengths and needs. Early intervention can make a big difference. Common approaches include:
list: Speech and language therapy, including alternative communication (AAC)
Occupational therapy and sensory support
Behavioural and developmental therapies
Special education and inclusive school support
Parent training and family support
Medical care for related conditions such as sleep problems or epilepsy

sections.title: Living with autism
paragraphs: With understanding, acceptance and the right support, autistic children grow, learn and build meaningful lives. An inclusive society — at school, in the clinic and in everyday life — is one of the most powerful forms of help.

rare.title: Rare diseases
rare.lead: A disease is called rare when it affects fewer than 1 in 2,000 people. There are more than 6,000 known rare diseases, and about 70% of them begin in childhood. Here we introduce some of them in plain language.

items.name: PMM2-CDG
items.text: The most common type of CDG, caused by changes in the PMM2 gene. It often causes low muscle tone, crossed eyes, balance problems and developmental delay, and can affect the liver, heart and blood clotting.

items.name: MPI-CDG
items.text: A type of CDG that mainly affects the liver and gut, causing diarrhoea, low blood sugar and clotting problems. Unlike most CDG types, it can be treated with oral mannose — which is why early diagnosis matters.

items.name: Rett syndrome
items.text: A genetic condition, usually caused by changes in the MECP2 gene, that mostly affects girls. After a period of typical development, children lose purposeful hand use and speech, and develop repetitive hand movements.

items.name: Angelman syndrome
items.text: Caused by loss of function of the UBE3A gene on chromosome 15. Children have severe speech delay, balance problems, seizures, and often a very happy, excitable personality.

items.name: Phelan-McDermid syndrome
items.text: Caused by a deletion at the end of chromosome 22 (22q13) or changes in the SHANK3 gene. It causes low muscle tone, delayed or absent speech and developmental delay, and is often associated with autism.

items.name: Fragile X syndrome
items.text: The most common inherited cause of intellectual disability, caused by changes in the FMR1 gene. It can cause learning difficulties, anxiety and hyperactivity, and many affected children are also autistic.

about.title: Born from a family’s journey
about.lead: The Foundation for CDG Syndrome and Autism was created by parents who know from their own experience how hard the road to a rare diagnosis can be.

events.title: Awareness campaigns
events.lead: Every year we join the global community on key awareness days — to tell our children’s stories, share knowledge and bring people together.

items.title: World CDG Awareness Day
items.text: On 16 May, families, doctors and researchers around the world raise awareness of congenital disorders of glycosylation. It is a day to share stories, support research and help more children get an early diagnosis.

items.title: World Autism Awareness Day
items.text: 2 April is the United Nations’ World Autism Awareness Day. We use it to promote understanding, acceptance and inclusion of autistic children and adults in every part of life.

beneficiary.title: Apply for support
beneficiary.lead: If your child is living with CDG, autism or another rare disease and your family needs help with diagnostics, therapy, treatment, medication or equipment, you can apply to the foundation.
who: Parents or legal guardians of a child (under 18) with CDG, autism or another rare disease
Families who need help covering costs that are not paid by the state or insurance
Children with a confirmed diagnosis or undergoing diagnostic investigation

steps.title: Fill in the form
steps.text: Provide information about the child, the parent or guardian, the family’s finances and the child’s medical condition.

steps.title: Describe the need
steps.text: Tell us what support you need — therapy, consultation, treatment, medication or equipment — and the amount requested.

steps.title: Attach documents
steps.text: Prepare medical documents, the child’s photos and other supporting files.

steps.title: Review and contact
steps.text: Our team reviews each application carefully and contacts the family about next steps.

docs: Medical records confirming the diagnosis (doctor’s conclusion, genetic test results)
Invoices or cost estimates for the requested therapy, treatment or equipment
Identity documents of the child and parent / guardian
Photos of the child (with consent for their use)
Proof of any other assistance the family already receives
